notes:
Task and constraints: Enumerate all directed paths from node zero to the final node.
Idea: Depth-first search follows each outgoing edge while maintaining the active route.
Technique and why it applies: The target case copies the route into results; popping after recursion restores the prior route for sibling branches.
Invariant: step is the current route, while res holds independent copies of completed paths.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty acyclic graph; dead ends simply yield no completed path.
Complexity: Runtime depends on the number and lengths of paths; recursion storage is O(V).

Task and constraints: Enumerate every path in a directed acyclic graph from source zero to target n-1.
Idea: Recursive DFS explores each neighbor, appending before recursion and popping afterward.
Technique and why it applies: The target case copies path so later backtracking cannot mutate stored answers.
Invariant: path is the active route; result contains independent copies of successful routes.
Edge cases: Acyclicity prevents infinite recursion; nodes that cannot reach target add no answer.
Complexity: Output-sensitive time depends on explored edges and returned path lengths; recursion space is O(V).

Task and constraints: Find the smallest rotation index with the highest array score.
Idea: A heap tracks score thresholds as the rotation increases one step at a time.
Technique and why it applies: Old thresholds are removed and the moved element's wrapped threshold is inserted.
Invariant: qualified is intended to represent elements scoring for the current rotation.
Edge cases: heappush and heappop lack imports in this snippet; threshold bookkeeping needs correctness checking.
Complexity: Intended heap operations take O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the earliest rotation giving the maximum score.
Idea: A difference array records score-change boundaries, then prefix sums recover scores.
Technique and why it applies: Each element decrements the score at its change position; accumulation updates all rotations.
Invariant: After accumulation, change[i] represents the score for rotation i up to a constant offset.
Edge cases: An empty array is outside normal constraints; index(max(...)) chooses the earliest maximum.
Complexity: The scans take O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the champagne amount in glass (r,c) after pouring at the top.
Idea: Simulate rows, keeping at most one unit per glass and splitting overflow evenly.
Technique and why it applies: Overflow from a glass is added to both children in the next row.
Invariant: quantity records incoming amounts before each glass is capped at one unit.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without an import; processing stops when a row has no overflow.
Complexity: Through row r, time and dictionary space are O(r²).

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps to make two sequences strictly increasing.
Idea: Memoized recursion tries leaving the current pair unchanged or swapping it.
Technique and why it applies: Each choice checks current values against the previous pair and charges one for a swap.
Invariant: solve tracks index, prior values, and the prior swap flag.
Edge cases: The memo key includes only index and flag although transitions depend on prior values, so caching may be incorrect; -1 assumes values exceed -1.
Complexity: Intended memo states are O(n), with O(n) recursion depth.

Task and constraints: Minimize swaps so arrays A and B are both strictly increasing.
Idea: Rolling DP tracks costs ending with the current pair swapped or unswapped.
Technique and why it applies: Direct comparisons carry forward the same state; cross-comparisons switch states and charge one swap.
Invariant: Alternating slots hold minimum costs for each state at the latest index.
Edge cases: Both arrays are assumed equal and nonempty; a single element correctly needs zero swaps.
Complexity: Each index uses constant work, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Find nodes from which every path eventually reaches a terminal node.
Idea: DFS tracks the active recursion path and rejects a node revisited within that path.
Technique and why it applies: Already-safe nodes are reused; successful recursion removes the current node from the path and marks it safe.
Invariant: loops contains the active path and ans contains terminal or verified safe nodes.
Edge cases: List membership is linear and repeated DFS can be costly; recursion can reach O(V) depth.
Complexity: Repeated exploration may cost O(V(V+E)) or more with list-membership overhead; space is O(V).

Task and constraints: Return the number of bricks falling after each hit, excluding the directly hit brick.
Idea: Apply hits, union remaining adjacent bricks, then reverse hits using union-find.
Technique and why it applies: A virtual roof joins top-row bricks; restoring a brick measures growth in the roof component.
Invariant: DSU components represent connectivity, and the roof component represents stable bricks.
Edge cases: Repeated hits on already empty cells return zero; grid is mutated in place.
Complexity: With path compression, work is approximately O((RC+H) α(RC)) and space O(RC).

Task and constraints: Count distinct Morse encodings of lowercase words.
Idea: Translate each character and count complete encodings as dictionary keys.
Technique and why it applies: The first occurrence creates a key and duplicates reuse it; only key count is returned.
Invariant: cnt has one key per distinct transformation encountered.
Edge cases: The mapping assumes lowercase letters; stored duplicate counts are irrelevant to the final answer.
Complexity: Total character processing is O(total characters), with space proportional to encoded text.

Task and constraints: Count distinct Morse encodings of supplied words.
Idea: Join Morse strings for each word and insert the result into a set.
Technique and why it applies: Set deduplication merges different words that produce the same encoded sequence.
Invariant: lookup contains the distinct encodings processed so far.
Edge cases: The table assumes lowercase letters; an empty word contributes the empty encoding once.
Complexity: Encoding takes O(total characters) time and set storage is proportional to distinct encoded lengths.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a nonempty proper subset has the same average as the whole array.
Idea: DP sets record achievable sums indexed by the number of selected items.
Technique and why it applies: Descending subset-size updates prevent reusing the current item in the same iteration.
Invariant: DP[k] contains sums achievable with exactly k processed values.
Edge cases: Sorting mutates the input; float division may be imprecise, and only sizes through half are checked.
Complexity: Reachable-sum sets can grow exponentially, so time and memory depend on distinct sums.

Task and constraints: Check whether an array can be split into subsets with equal average.
Idea: First test possible subset sizes, then track reachable sums for each size.
Technique and why it applies: A subset of size i matches the average when total*i is divisible by n and its sum equals total*i/n.
Invariant: sums[i] stores achievable sums using exactly i values from the processed prefix.
Edge cases: The call possible(n,s) reverses the helper's intended arguments total and n, so valid inputs may be rejected incorrectly.
Complexity: Subset-sum state growth may be exponential in the number of values.

Task and constraints: Return line count and final width when writing a string under a 100-unit limit.
Idea: Accumulate each character width and start a new line when the sum exceeds 100.
Technique and why it applies: On overflow, the code increments line count and resets width to the current character's width.
Invariant: px is current line width and l counts started lines.
Edge cases: The print(ord(...)) statement produces debugging output; a character wider than 100 is still placed on a line.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return line count and final width under the 100-unit line limit.
Idea: Scan characters, adding each width and starting a new line when the limit is exceeded.
Technique and why it applies: The result starts at one line and zero width; after overflow the current character begins the next line.
Invariant: result[0] tracks line count and result[1] tracks current width.
Edge cases: The implementation assumes lowercase letters and widths indexed by alphabet position; it does not print debugging output.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Maximize building-height increases without changing row and column skylines.
Idea: Compute row maxima and column maxima, then sum each cell's allowed increase.
Technique and why it applies: A cell may rise only to the smaller of its row and column maxima.
Invariant: mxr and mxc preserve skyline limits from the original grid.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular grid and visits cells during accumulation.
Complexity: Computing maxima and summing cells takes O(RC) time and O(R+C) extra space.

Task and constraints: Maximize total height increase while preserving the original city skylines.
Idea: Calculate row and column maxima, then sum permitted increases cell by cell.
Technique and why it applies: The final height is bounded by both skyline maxima, so increase is their minimum minus current height.
Invariant: row_maxes and col_maxes preserve the original row and column limits.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular grid; zip(*grid) derives its columns.
Complexity: The scans take O(RC) time and O(R+C) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the probability soup A empties first, with simultaneous emptying worth one-half.
Idea: Scale amounts into 25-unit servings and memoize probabilities for remaining amount pairs.
Technique and why it applies: Four equally likely operations lead to smaller states, whose probabilities are averaged.
Invariant: dp(i,j) is the probability A empties first from scaled amounts i and j.
Edge cases: For n above 4451 the implementation returns 1.0 as an approximation; memoization avoids repeated subproblems.
Complexity: There are O(m²) scaled states, giving O(m²) time and space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the probability soup A empties first under four serving operations.
Idea: Memoize a recursive probability function over scaled amounts for both soups.
Technique and why it applies: Average the four next-state probabilities; base cases handle simultaneous emptying or one soup finishing first.
Invariant: lookup[(a,b)] stores the probability for that remaining-amount state.
Edge cases: Amounts are rounded up to 25-unit servings; N at least 4800 returns 1.0 as an approximation.
Complexity: For scaled amount m, there are O(m²) states and O(m²) memo space.

Task and constraints: Count words stretchable to match s by expanding repeated-character runs.
Idea: Compress each string into its run-character sequence and run lengths, then compare aligned runs.
Technique and why it applies: Character sequences must match; a target run can be longer only when length is at least three, and a word run cannot exceed it.
Invariant: s_split and s_array encode target run characters and lengths.
Edge cases: Empty-input branches return booleans rather than counts; operator precedence affects the compound run check.
Complexity: Each word is processed linearly; total time is O(total characters), with temporary compressed-word space.
